title: Cognitive Mobility: Ein Modell professioneller Denkarbeit unter KI-Bedingungen
abstract: Der vorliegende Text entwickelt das Modell der Kognitiven Mobilität (Cognitive Mobility) als Versuch, professionelle Denkarbeit unter Bedingungen dauerhafter KI-Mitwirkung zu beschreiben. Ausgangspunkt ist nicht die Frage, ob KI grundsätzlich Arbeit schneller macht, sondern wie sie die Bedingungen verändert, unter denen professionelles Denken entsteht, sich bewegt und sich selbst überprüft. Im Zentrum steht die Annahme, dass KI nicht angemessen als bloßes Werkzeug zur Entlastung beschrieben werden kann. Sie verändert die Verteilung kognitiver Last und damit die Bedingungen professioneller Denkarbeit. KI kann den Zugang zu komplexen Denkoperationen erleichtern, Material erschließen, Perspektiven öffnen und professionelle Handlungsmöglichkeiten erweitern. Zugleich erzeugt genau diese Erleichterung ein neues Risiko: Wenn der Zugang zum Denken friktionsärmer wird, kann auch der Unterschied zwischen eigener Urteilsbildung und maschinell erzeugter Anschlussfähigkeit verwischen. Diesen gerichteten Zug KI-gestützter Arbeitsumgebungen zur Reduktion kognitiver Reibung fasst das Modell als Cognitive Gravity — seinen zentralen Risikobegriff: Man nutzt KI nicht einfach; man bewegt sich in einem Feld, das eine Richtung hat. Das Modell unterscheidet vier Modi der Mensch-KI-Kooperation: Cognitive Relief, Cognitive Offloading, Cognitive Augmentation und Cognitive Transformation. Sie sind keine Aufstiegsstufen, sondern funktionale Formen kognitiver Lastverteilung, die produktiv sein, aber auch kippen können. Quer zu diesen Modi steht Cognitive Recognition als Querschnittskompetenz: die Fähigkeit, KI-generierte Muster kritisch zu lesen. Ohne dieses Loading droht eine Verschiebung vom Werkzeug zum Denkersatz. Drift und Sedation werden als Mechanismen verstanden, über die Atrophy schleichend entsteht. Mit geliehener Souveränität beschreibt der Beitrag zudem eine Wirkung von Cognitive Gravity auf Selbstbild und Auftreten: die Diskrepanz zwischen Auftrittsgewissheit und epistemischer Deckung. Das Modell positioniert KI als kognitives Exoskelett. Ein Exoskelett ersetzt den Körper nicht; es stützt, stabilisiert und erweitert ihn. English Abstract This working paper develops the model of Cognitive Mobility as an attempt to describe professional cognition under conditions of sustained human-AI cooperation. Its starting point is not whether AI simply makes work faster, but how it changes the conditions under which professional thinking emerges, moves, and examines itself. At the centre of the model is the assumption that AI cannot adequately be described as a mere tool of relief. It changes the distribution of cognitive load and, with it, the conditions of professional cognition. AI can facilitate access to complex cognitive operations, open up material, generate perspectives, and expand professional agency. At the same time, precisely this facilitation creates a new risk: as access to thinking becomes less frictional, the distinction between one's own judgement and machine-generated connective plausibility can begin to blur. The model names this directed pull of AI-supported working environments toward the reduction of cognitive friction Cognitive Gravity — its central risk concept: one does not simply use AI; one moves in a field that has a direction. The model distinguishes four modes of human-AI cooperation: Cognitive Relief, Cognitive Offloading, Cognitive Augmentation, and Cognitive Transformation. These are not stages of progress, but functional forms of cognitive load distribution that can be productive, yet can also tip into risk. Across these modes, Cognitive Recognition functions as a transversal competence: the ability to read AI-generated patterns critically. A central prerequisite for productive AI use is Cognitive Loading: the independent development of subject-specific, linguistic, and epistemic structures before these are relieved or extended by AI. Without such loading, AI risks shifting from tool to substitute structure. Cognitive Gravity can foster Cognitive Atrophy: the weakening or non-development of cognitive abilities through outsourcing before one's own structures have been built. Drift and Sedation are understood as mechanisms through which Atrophy can emerge gradually. With borrowed sovereignty, the paper further describes an effect of Cognitive Gravity on self-image and demeanour: the discrepancy between the confidence of one's appearance and its epistemic coverage. Empirically, this perspective resonates with Hoffmann et al. (2026). Their survey of 4,048 students on academic writing with AI shows that productive use and perceived risks to one's own thinking processes coexist. The authors document widespread AI use, the delegation of central writing and reading operations, and concerns about unlearning critical thinking. Their reference to a possible "tipping point" is particularly significant: if students write their first academic texts already with AI, they may lack a sense of what is lost through extensive delegation. Cognitive Loading thus becomes not only a prerequisite for productive AI use, but an educational task under conditions in which Cognitive Offloading is available from the outset. The model conceptualizes AI as a cognitive exoskeleton. An exoskeleton does not replace the body; it supports, stabilizes, and extends it. Precisely for this reason, the question arises which cognitive muscles must continue to be exercised so that support does not turn into dependency. The exoskeleton does not only carry — it also pulls. Cognitive Mobility is therefore not the absence of Cognitive Gravity, but the ability to move in an epistemically self-determined way under its pull.

title: Enhancing Compliance Training with LLM-Powered Conversational Agents: A Design Science Evaluation of FERPA Education
abstract: Compliance training is mandatory in many organizations, yet often experienced as tedious, passive, and quickly forgotten. In higher education, FERPA training is a high-stakes example: institutions must educate employees and affiliates on legally constrained information practices, but training is typically delivered through one-way video or slide-based modules that learners complete as a ''check-the-box'' requirement. Drawing on Constructivist Learning Theory, Self-Determination Theory, and Cognitive Load Theory, we use a Design Science Research (DSR) approach to develop and evaluate two FERPA training artifacts that cover the same content but differ in delivery: (1) a baseline, push-oriented video module used by the institution, and (2) a pull-oriented, LLM-powered chatbot tutor implemented via Dialogflow CX and a web frontend. We evaluate both artifacts through a qualitative field study with participants who require FERPA training, using semi-structured interviews and reflexive thematic analysis. Findings suggest that the chatbot format increases perceived learner control, sustains attention through interaction, and supports deeper processing by enabling targeted questioning and scenario-based application. We contribute (1) a set of reusable design principles for LLM-enabled compliance tutoring in regulated contexts, and (2) qualitative evidence about how conversational delivery reshapes learner experience in mandatory compliance education.

title: Allergen Detection in Food Labels Using Transformer-Based Named Entity Recognition
abstract: Food allergies pose serious health risks, making accurate identification of allergen information on food labels essential for consumer safety. However, food packaging text is often difficult to interpret due to diverse layouts, multilingual terminology, and inconsistent formatting. This study addresses the problem by formulating allergen detection from food labels as a Named Entity Recognition (NER) task and applying transformer-based Natural Language Processing models to identify allergen entities from packaging text. A domain-specific dataset was constructed from real-world food labels, where text was extracted using Optical Character Recognition, manually cleaned, and annotated with allergen entities following the BIO tagging scheme. Transformer-based NER models, including IndoBERT, Multilingual BERT (mBERT), and XLMRoBERTa, were fine-tuned and evaluated using standard NER metrics. The results demonstrate that transformer-based NER is effective for allergen detection in food label text, with mBERT achieving the best balance between precision and recall. These findings highlight the potential of transformer-based NER models to support automated allergen detection and improve food label accessibility for consumers. The best-performing model (mBERT) achieved an entity-level F1-score of 0.686.

title: Quantum computing in image processing: A review of applications, models, and prospects
abstract: Quantum computing is increasingly being viewed as a promising direction for the future of image processing. Conventional approaches to image classification, enhancement, compression, and restoration, although highly developed, often struggle with scalability, computational complexity, and data security—especially when processing high-dimensional or sensitive visual information. This survey explores how quantum computing can help address these limitations through quantum image representation models such as FRQI and NEQR, variational quantum circuits, and hybrid quantum–classical architectures. The primary objective of this review is to present a clear and structured overview of the current state of quantum image processing (QIP). It discusses foundational representation models, emerging hybrid learning techniques, available software frameworks and simulators, benchmarking practices, and practical applications in areas such as medical imaging, remote sensing, and biometric security. Particular attention is given to solutions that are feasible on today’s NISQ-era hardware, including hybrid architectures and quantum-secured image processing schemes. The survey concludes by identifying existing challenges and outlining realistic future research directions. Overall, it emphasizes the practical importance of hybrid models, the need for standardized quantum-oriented benchmarks, and the growing potential of quantum-based security mechanisms for safeguarding visual data.

title: Orthogonal Polynomials and the MacWilliams Transform for Permutation-Invariant Qudit Codes
abstract: We derive an explicit formula for the intrinsic MacWilliams transform for permutation-invariant qudit codes. Such codes naturally live in symmetric power representations, where the relevant error sectors are determined by the irreducible decomposition of the conjugation action on the associated operator space. Using the multiplicity-free structure of this decomposition and the corresponding intertwiner algebra, we identify the intrinsic MacWilliams matrix with a finite Racah transform. The entries are given by a terminating hypergeometric series, and the rows of the matrix are Racah orthogonal polynomials with parameters determined explicitly by the block length and local dimension. Computing the spectrum of the degree-one twirl reveals that this spectrum lies on an affine quadratic lattice. Then we derive a tridiagonal multiplication rule from the representation theory of the adjoint sector. As consequences, we obtain closed-form orthogonality, detailed-balance, and involutivity identities for the transform. The resulting formula supplies an explicit MacWilliams matrix for computing linear programming bounds on permutation-invariant qudit codes.

title: Quantifying and Mitigating Premature Closure in Frontier LLMs
abstract: Premature closure, or committing to a conclusion before sufficient information is available, is a recognized contributor to diagnostic error but remains underexamined in large language models (LLMs). We define LLM premature closure as inappropriate commitment under uncertainty: providing an answer, recommendation, or clinical guidance when the safer response would be clarification, abstention, escalation, or refusal. We evaluated five frontier LLMs across structured and open-ended medical tasks. In MedQA (n = 500) and AfriMed-QA (n = 490) questions where the correct choice had been removed, models still selected an answer at high rates, with baseline false-action rates of 55-81% and 53-82%, respectively. In open-ended evaluation, models gave inappropriate answers on an average of 30% of 861 HealthBench questions and 78% of 191 physician-authored adversarial queries. Safety-oriented prompting reduced premature closure across models, but residual failure persisted, highlighting the need to evaluate whether medical LLMs know when not to answer.

title: When Answers Stray from Questions: Hallucination Detection via Question-Answer Orthogonal Decomposition
abstract: Hallucination detection in large language models (LLMs) requires balancing accu racy, efficiency, and robustness to distribution shift. Black-box consistency methods are effective but demand repeated inference; single-pass white-box probes are effi cient yet treat answer representations in isolation, often degrading sharply under domain shift. We propose QAOD (Question-Answer Orthogonal Decomposition), a single-pass framework that projects away the question-aligned direction from the answer representation to obtain a question-orthogonal component that suppresses domain-conditioned variation. To identify informative signals, QAOD further selects layers via diversity-penalized Fisher scoring and discriminative neurons via Fisher importance. To address both in-domain detection and cross-domain generalization, we design two complementary probing strategies: pairing the or thogonal component with question context yields a joint probe that maximizes in-domain discriminability, while using the orthogonal component alone preserves domain-agnostic factuality signals for robust transfer. QAOD's joint probe achieves the best in-domain AUROC across all evaluated model-dataset pairs, while the orthogonal-only probe delivers the strongest OOD transfer, surpassing the best white-box baseline by up to 21% on BioASQ at under 25% of generation cost.

title: Quantum optical synthesis of high-dimensional ultrafast frequency-bin qudits
abstract: Frequency modes of light are one of the most promising platforms that provide access to high-dimensional quantum states amongst different photonic degrees of freedom capable of high-dimensionality, enabling robust, error-tolerant, and scalable quantum optical information systems. We demonstrate engineering of precisely controlled two-photon high-dimensional states entangled in frequency through time-domain Fourier optical synthesis. We generate and convert a continuous broadband frequency-entangled state into a large range of discrete frequency bins suitable for ITU standards, with spacings ranging from 12.5 GHz to 750 GHz, and observe spectral anticorrelations over 38 frequency bins, including intra-bin pure states at a 100 GHz bin spacing. We characterize the full quantum state dimensionality via Schmidt decomposition and observe lower bounds on the frequency-binned Hilbert-space dimensionalities of at least 289, formed by two entangled qudits with dimension 17. Furthermore, we demonstrate quantum nonlocality via frequency correlations in a transmission experiment over a campus-scale two-node fiber network. This work represents a crucial step towards building a versatile and relatively simple way of generating precisely controlled high-dimensional spectral qudits, with the potential of harnessing in wavelength-multiplexed quantum networks, high-dimensional information processing, and communication of quantum states specifically, and fiber-optic quantum remote sensing.

title: nlq-validator: Lightweight Natural Language Query Validator
abstract: A lightweight Natural Language Query (NLQ) validator that keeps LLM assistants on-topic. Train it on example questions and it will accept in-domain queries while rejecting off-topic ones using TF-IDF scoring or semantic embeddings. Supports incremental retraining, threshold calibration, and automatic training-data generation via Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Mistral, Grok, and Perplexity.

title: "ATX-1 v2.3: AEGIS Threat Matrix for Agentic AI Systems"
abstract: "ATX-1 (AEGIS Threat Matrix) is a structured adversarial knowledge base cataloguing failure modes of autonomous AI agents operating without governance constraints. Unlike MITRE ATT&CK (which targets human adversaries) or MITRE ATLAS (which targets adversaries against AI systems), ATX-1 addresses a distinct threat class: AI agents that act outside their governance boundaries through structural capability without authority, not through external compromise. Composite scenarios in which external triggers (e.g., indirect prompt injection) flow into the agent's action surface are explicitly in scope.Version 2.3 removes the `severity` field from technique definitions in alignment with MITRE ATT&CK and ATLAS conventions, which leave contextual scoring to the consumer. title: Quantum noise in ranging with optical pulses
abstract: Optical frequency combs combine ultrashort pulse duration and phase stability, making them powerful resources for high-precision ranging even when affected by atmospheric dispersion. It has been established that by classical modal engineering and mode-sensitive detection, sensitivity to distance at the standard limit can be achieved; however, attaining improved uncertainties by the use of squeezing has not been explored. Here, we apply an effective Hamiltonian framework to the problem of ranging with quantum frequency combs in order to derive the associated precision bounds for distance estimation. The problem needs addressing of the pulse shape and its quantum properties at once. The analysis reveals that quantum solutions may be appealing mostly for short-distance applications.

title: EaSFE: Scalable and Efficient Feature Engineering for Boosting Machine Learning Performance
abstract: Feature engineering plays a critical role in machine learning (ML), but existing methods often struggle with high computational cost and limited scalability when applied to large-scale and sparse datasets. In this article, we propose EaSFE, an efficient and scalable feature engineering framework that unifies feature generation, filtering, and evaluation in an end-to-end manner. EaSFE is designed to efficiently construct and select informative features while explicitly considering computational and memory constraints. To achieve scalability, EaSFE incorporates parallel and distributed execution mechanisms, as well as a chunk-based data processing strategy that enables memory-efficient feature engineering on large datasets. In addition, EaSFE adopts tailored storage and execution strategies to handle high-dimensional sparse data effectively. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that EaSFE consistently improves predictive performance (e.g., 5% accuracy improvement in poker ) while substantially enhancing efficiency (i.e., over 10x speedup) compared to existing feature engineering methods. In addition, EaSFE is demonstrated to scale to large and sparse datasets, successfully handling datasets with over 119 million training instances and 54 million features.

title: Learning from scratch: variational dynamic-driven reward learning for continuous control
abstract: Intrinsic reward-based learning has become a popular topic in reinforcement learning. Although previous studies have made strides in discrete control, scaling it to continuous control tasks still remains challenging. To remedy this issue, we propose a Variational Dynamic-Driven Reward Learning method (VD2RL) to better extend intrinsic reward-based learning to continuous control. Specifically, VD2RL introduces an environment-dependent constraint to encourage learning informative latent representation of dynamics, shedding new light on the usage of latent capacity for continuous control. Then, VD2RL proposes a novel information-bottleneck guided reward function relating to behavior diversity and state novelty, which is preferable for continuous control. Experiments show that VD2RL contrives more effective learning in challenging continuous control tasks than prior methods.
